meaning: The default daytime greeting until early afternoon — used between strangers too.
From about 4pm onwards. Shopkeepers will say it back the second you walk in.
Stress the last syllable. Pair with a small nod — it goes a long way on the bus.
Same word both ways. Drivers use it to mean 'go ahead, sit down'.
Confusingly short — it sounds like 'no' in English, but it means yes.
Often paired with a small upward chin lift instead of shaking the head.
What the blue Aloya pins mark. Ask a local 'πού είναι η στάση;' — where is the stop?
Long word, worth learning — the only word older Cypriots use for the city bus.
Cash to the driver, or use a Motion card. Around €1.50 for a single ride.
Works for a coffee, a bus fare, a souvenir — the most useful three-word phrase.
Tap shoulder, say this, and Cypriots will move to let you off the bus.
Informal, singular. Use 'γεια σας' (yia sas) for groups or older people.
Buses with 'paralía' on the destination board are heading to the seafront.
Tap water is fine across Cyprus — most of it is desalinated seawater.
Ask for 'kafés kipriakós, métrios' — Cypriot coffee, medium-sweet. Served with cold water.
The grilled cheese. Salty, squeaky, and on practically every Cypriot menu.
Sunday lunch in Cyprus. Whole cuts of lamb or pork on a long, slow rotisserie.
Drivers shout this as the doors close. Locals shout it before everything fun.
Cypriots drop this into every other sentence. Friendly, low-key, never formal.
The Cypriot pace philosophy. Whatever it is, it'll happen — just not in a hurry.
You'll hear this on arrival at hotels, restaurants, and friends' homes.
Safe to say after the first bite of anything. The cook will beam.
Pair with a place name: 'pú íne i paralía?' — where is the beach?
Means 'one moment' in conversation, and 'one minute to departure' on bus screens.
Soft, open-ended. In Cyprus, 'argótera' could mean five minutes or five hours.
A one-word answer for sunsets, food, weddings, and a well-timed bus.
Polite way to order in a taverna. Follow with 'éna kafé' for one coffee.
Combine with a small writing-in-the-air gesture and the bill will arrive.
Said only before sleeping, never just leaving a place. For that, use 'γεια σας'.
Glass clink, eye contact, this phrase. Skipping the eye contact is bad form.
